sugestoes.texto: The backup-code branch authenticates the user without verifying the password because the password check at line 121 is skipped whenever `credentials.totpCode` is truthy. WHAT: An attacker with a stolen backup code can log in without the password by submitting any non-empty `totpCode` alongside the `backupCode`. WHY: Static backup codes are easier to steal than time-based TOTP, and this PR makes the pre-existing password-skip newly exploitable. HOW: Verify the password unconditionally before entering either 2FA branch, or add an explicit password check inside the backup-code branch.

The component in `BackupCode.tsx` is exported as `function TwoFactor` instead of `BackupCode`. WHAT: Wrong component identifier/copy-paste error. WHY: React DevTools and maintainers see the wrong name, and named imports from this module would fail. HOW: Rename the function to `BackupCode`.

Backup-code comparison is case-sensitive while generated codes are lowercase hex. WHAT: A user-typed uppercase backup code fails `indexOf` and is rejected as incorrect. WHY: Codes are generated with `crypto.randomBytes(5).toString("hex")` (lowercase) and the input is not normalized. HOW: Normalize the stripped input with `.toLowerCase()` before `indexOf`.

Same case-sensitivity issue in the disable-2FA backup-code path. WHAT: A valid backup code typed in uppercase is rejected. WHY: `indexOf` compares against lowercase hex codes without normalizing input. HOW: Normalize `req.body.backupCode.replaceAll("-", "").toLowerCase()` before comparison.

Used backup codes are replaced with `null` and the array is re-encrypted, so the DB field stays non-empty even after every code is consumed. WHAT: When all backup codes are used, `MissingBackupCodes` is not thrown; the user receives `IncorrectBackupCode`. WHY: The guard only checks `!user.backupCodes`, but an encrypted array of nulls is truthy. HOW: Filter out `null` entries before re-encrypting, and return `MissingBackupCodes` when no valid entries remain.

WHAT: The backup-code authentication branch does not verify the user's password when `credentials.totpCode` is also present. WHY: The preceding password check is gated on `!credentials.totpCode`, so an attacker who knows a backup code can bypass password verification by sending any non-empty `totpCode`, causing `authorize` to accept the backup code and issue a session. HOW: Verify the password unconditionally (when the user has a CAL password) before entering either 2FA branch, or perform the password check inside the backup-code branch.

WHAT: Consuming a backup code is a non-atomic read-modify-write on the encrypted `backupCodes` array. WHY: Two concurrent login requests can both decrypt the original array, find the same valid code, both update it to `null`, and both succeed, violating the single-use guarantee for backup codes. HOW: Use a compare-and-swap update (e.g., a transaction or raw SQL that only matches rows whose decrypted array still contains the supplied code) or re-verify after the write.

WHAT: `useState([])` has no element type, so `backupCodes` is inferred as `never[]`. WHY: TypeScript rejects assigning `body.backupCodes` (`string[]`) to the setter and rejects calling `.slice` in `formatBackupCode`, causing a build/type error. HOW: Change the state declaration to `useState<string[]>([])`.

WHAT: Backup code comparison is case-sensitive while generated codes are lowercase hex. WHY: A user typing a code in uppercase (e.g., from the placeholder or a printed copy) is rejected as incorrect even when the code is valid. HOW: Normalize the submitted code to lowercase before comparing, e.g. `credentials.backupCode.replaceAll('-','').toLowerCase()`.

WHAT: The disable-2FA backup code check is case-sensitive while generated codes are lowercase hex. WHY: A valid backup code entered in uppercase is rejected as incorrect. HOW: Normalize `req.body.backupCode.replaceAll('-','').toLowerCase()` before calling `indexOf`.

issues.descricao: The credentials authorize() skips the password check when any totpCode is present, and the new backup-code branch never validates that totpCode, so a backup code plus a dummy totpCode logs in without the account password.

comentarios.texto: The new backup-code branch authenticates without guaranteeing the password check ran: password verification at line 121 is gated on `!credentials.totpCode`, and the branch at line 131 triggers on any truthy `credentials.backupCode` regardless of that gate. A POST to the credentials callback supplying a valid backup code together with any non-empty totpCode therefore takes the backup branch (skipping TOTP validation) while line 121 skips password verification — granting a session using only a second-factor backup code, with no account password. Require the password check before the backup branch, or include backupCode in the guard at line 121 (e.g. `if (user.password && !credentials.totpCode && !credentials.backupCode)`).

The backup-code branch accepts a valid backup code even when an arbitrary nonempty totpCode has skipped password verification. The preceding guards at lines 113–125 trust the presence of totpCode, but this new branch does not validate it, allowing a holder of a backup code to log in to a password account without knowing its password by submitting both fields. Require password verification for backup-code authentication rather than allowing an unverified totpCode to bypass it.

WHAT: The new backup-code login branch authenticates without verifying the password when credentials also contain any totpCode value (password check at line 121 is skipped when totpCode is truthy, and the backup branch never checks it). WHY: An attacker holding only a backup code can add a dummy totpCode to the credentials callback and log in without the password, reducing two factors to one. HOW: Verify the password whenever backupCode is used (or decouple the password check from totpCode presence).

issues.descricao: After enabling 2FA, onEnable is only called from the backup-codes Close button; dismissing the dialog by Escape/overlay never notifies the parent, so the settings page keeps showing 2FA disabled.

comentarios.texto: On a successful enable (response.status === 200) the modal no longer calls onEnable(); it only advances to SetupStep.DisplayBackupCodes, and onEnable() is now invoked solely from the 'close' button (line 269). If the user dismisses the Dialog via ESC or an overlay click, DialogContent's onOpenChange fires (wired to a plain setEnableModalOpen toggle at apps/web/pages/settings/security/two-factor-auth.tsx:64 and the conditional render at apps/web/components/security/TwoFactorAuthSection.tsx:36), so onEnable never runs. The parent callbacks (setEnableModalOpen(false) + utils.viewer.me.invalidate() / setEnabled(true)) are skipped, leaving the 2FA Switch unchecked and the UI showing 2FA as disabled even though the server has enabled it. Call onEnable() from the dismiss path (onOpenChange) or when transitioning into DisplayBackupCodes, not only from the Close button.

Successful enablement no longer invokes onEnable until the backup-code screen's explicit Close button is clicked. Dismissing that screen through the dialog's onOpenChange instead only closes it in the parent and does not invalidate viewer.me, leaving the settings switch showing disabled even though the server has enabled 2FA. Ensure dismissal after successful enablement also invokes the completion callback and resets the setup state.

After a successful enable, `onEnable()` is no longer called and is only called from the backup-codes Close button. If the user dismisses the dialog by Escape or overlay click (`onOpenChange`) while the codes are displayed, the parent is never notified that 2FA is enabled. The modal also keeps its step state and the plaintext backup codes. Call `onEnable` when 2FA is enabled, or make the dialog's `onOpenChange(false)` on the DisplayBackupCodes step run the same handler as Close, which resets state and clears `backupCodes`.

issues.descricao: Backup-code consumption is a non-atomic read-modify-write, so concurrent logins can accept the same backup code more than once or overwrite each other's removal.
issues.textoGolden: Because backupCodes are decrypted and mutated in memory before being written back, two concurrent login requests using the same backupCode could both pass this check and update, so a single backup code may effectively be accepted more than once if used concurrently, weakening the intended one-time-use semantics.

comentarios.texto: Backup-code consumption is a non-atomic read-modify-write: the code is validated with indexOf (line 144) and only then persisted via prisma.user.update (line 149), with no unique constraint or lock. Two concurrent login requests sending the same valid backup code both read the unchanged row, both pass the indexOf check, and both obtain a session, violating the 'each backup code can be used exactly once' invariant. Consume the code atomically (e.g. a conditional update on the raw encrypted value / a dedicated used-backup-codes table with a unique index) so only one request can succeed.

Backup-code consumption is a non-atomic read-modify-write, breaking the stated invariant that each backup code is single-use. Two concurrent login requests with the same backup code both read the same user.backupCodes array and both pass `index !== -1` before either `prisma.user.update` commits; both then persist a stale array (each nulling only its own index), so the code authenticates twice. Make consumption atomic (e.g. compare-and-swap on the encrypted value/updatedAt, a transaction with a conditional update, or an optimistic-locking retry) so exactly one request can claim a given code.

Backup-code consumption overwrites the encrypted list by user ID without checking that the stored list still matches the value read before verification. Concurrent requests can both authenticate with the same single-use code, and requests using different codes can overwrite each other's removals and restore a consumed code. Use a conditional atomic update matching the original backupCodes ciphertext and reject or retry authentication if no row was updated.

comentarios.texto: The light-theme value no longer matches the original. WHAT: `.topic-map h3` was `scale-color($primary, $lightness: 20%)` and now is `dark-light-choose(scale-color($primary, $lightness: 50%), scale-color($secondary, $lightness: 50%))` (20% → 50%). WHY: this visibly lightens the topic-map heading in the light theme; the desktop counterpart at desktop/topic-post.scss:321 correctly kept 20% (20/80), so mobile diverged. HOW: use `dark-light-choose(scale-color($primary, $lightness: 20%), scale-color($secondary, $lightness: 80%))`.

Original was scale-color($primary, $lightness: 20%). The conversion changed it to 50%/50%, but the desktop mirror of this rule (desktop/topic-post.scss h3) uses 20%/80%. The two files must agree; should be dark-light-choose(scale-color($primary, $lightness: 20%), scale-color($secondary, $lightness: 80%)).

This `h3` was originally `scale-color($primary, $lightness: 20%)`. The rewrite changed the light-theme argument to 50%, so the light theme renders the heading lighter than before; the correct pair is 20/80, not 50/50. The first argument must keep the original 20%.

issues.descricao: The comment describing the topic-list cell default color still names a plain scale-color($primary, 50%) rule that the PR replaced with dark-light-choose.

comentarios.texto: The comment at lines 72-74 states "the default for table cells in topic list is scale-color($primary, $lightness: 50%)", but the rule it documents was converted by this PR to `dark-light-choose(scale-color($primary, $lightness: X%), scale-color($secondary, $lightness: 100-X%))` (here for coldmap-high/med/low and in common/base/_topic-list.scss th/td). The prose still names a single `$primary` expression, so it no longer describes the code: a reader comparing the two will look for a plain `$primary` 50% rule that no longer exists. Update the comment to describe the dark-light-choose baseline (e.g. "is dark-light-choose(scale-color($primary, $lightness: 50%), scale-color($secondary, $lightness: 50%))").

issues.descricao: In dark themes the notification badge background becomes a lightened $secondary while its text stays $secondary, giving dark text on a dark background with poor contrast.

comentarios.texto: The dark-theme notification badge background now uses a lightened $secondary while its text still uses the unmodified $secondary. This puts dark text on a dark background for plain badges such as category unread counts in site-map.hbs:73; with $secondary black, the foreground is #000 and the background is approximately #4d4d4d (about 2.5:1 contrast), making the small count text difficult to read. Set the default badge foreground, including its &[href] rule, to a contrasting dark-theme color such as $primary when selecting this dark background.

sugestoes.texto: OAuth token exchange data is missing redirect_uri. WHAT: The POST to GitHub's access_token endpoint only sends code, client_id, and client_secret. WHY: GitHub requires the same redirect_uri in the token request when one was supplied to /authorize, so the flow will fail; the existing OAuth2CallbackView.get_token_params (identity/oauth2.py:273-280) includes it for this reason. HOW: Add "redirect_uri": absolute_uri(reverse("sentry-extension-setup", kwargs={"provider_id": "github"})) to the data dict.

Unprotected access to integration.metadata['sender']['login'] can raise KeyError. WHAT: The installer-vs-authenticated-user comparison reads nested keys without checking their existence. WHY: Integration rows may lack the 'sender' metadata (legacy installs or build_integration without a webhook sender), causing a 500 instead of the rendered error page. HOW: Guard the lookup, e.g., use integration.metadata.get('sender', {}).get('login') and treat a missing sender as a mismatch that returns the error response.

safe_urlopen is called outside the try/except that only wraps safe_urlread, so network errors from the GitHub token endpoint (ConnectionError, Timeout, etc.) propagate uncaught and surface as a 500 instead of the integration error page. Move safe_urlopen inside the try block, matching OAuth2CallbackView.exchange_token.

get_user_info calls raise_for_status() and can raise on a non-2xx /user response or request failure, but the call is unhandled and will return a 500 instead of the error page. Wrap get_user_info in the existing try/except or add explicit error handling and return error(request, self.active_organization).

OAuth state is set to pipeline.signature, which is a deterministic md5 of the pipeline view class names and therefore predictable and shared across all users/sessions. This defeats the CSRF protection of the OAuth callback and allows an attacker who can start a pipeline to forge a valid callback with their own authorization code, bypassing the new installer-vs-authenticated-user validation. Generate a per-session nonce (e.g., secrets.token_hex()), bind it to pipeline state, and compare the returned state against that stored value, as OAuth2LoginView does.

issues.descricao: error() calls _(error_short) on a variable and callers pass plain literals, so the short error strings are no longer extractable for translation.

comentarios.texto: The helper calls `_(error_short)` on a variable, and callers pass plain string literals. The translation extractor cannot see these strings, so the short error messages sent to the user are no longer translatable; the old code wrapped the literals directly in `_()`. Mark the literals with gettext_lazy at the call sites and the default, and pass them through without wrapping again.

error_short strings bypass translation extraction: _(error_short) uses a variable so makemessages cannot collect them. Wrap literals at definition/call sites, e.g. error_short=_("Invalid installation request.") and pass _("...") literals, then use data error value directly without re-wrapping.

Translate the short-message literals at their definition/call sites instead of calling `_(error_short)` on a variable. Django's message extraction cannot extract the default `"Invalid installation request."` or the plain-string arguments at the two call sites from this dynamic gettext invocation. The existing pending-deletion and already-installed messages previously appeared directly inside `_()`; this refactor removes their extraction sites, and the new default message cannot enter translation catalogs. Use a translated default and translated arguments, then place `error_short` directly into the payload so these user-facing errors remain localizable.

issues.descricao: The org parameter of error()/get_document_origin is actually the active-organization context, not an Organization, so the name is misleading.

comentarios.texto: The parameter is named `org` but the code treats it as the pipeline's active-organization context: it dereferences `org.organization` and every caller (error() and the GitHubInstallation sites) passes `self.active_organization`, not an Organization. The name misstates the argument's type/contract — a caller following the name and passing a real Organization would hit AttributeError on `.organization`. Rename the parameter (e.g. `active_organization`) and correct the corresponding name in `error()` at line 131 so the two signatures match what is actually passed.

issues.descricao: The GitHub OAuth state is pipeline.signature, a static md5 of the pipeline view names, instead of a per-attempt random nonce, so it gives no CSRF protection.
issues.textoGolden: OAuth state uses pipeline.signature (static) instead of a per-request random value

comentarios.texto: The OAuth state is pipeline.signature, which Pipeline.__init__ computes solely from pipeline view class names and therefore shares across all users and installation attempts. An attacker can obtain an OAuth code for their own GitHub account and send a callback using this known state to a victim with an active installation pipeline, binding the attacker's GitHub identity to the victim's flow instead of rejecting the forged callback. Generate a random per-attempt nonce, store it in pipeline state, and validate that nonce on the OAuth callback.

Do not use pipeline.signature as OAuth state. It is a deterministic MD5 of the pipeline identifiers, not an unpredictable nonce tied to this user's authorization attempt (the tests reuse it across users). An attacker can know the expected state and submit a callback containing a code authorized under the attacker's GitHub account, defeating the OAuth login-CSRF protection and the intended binding to the installing user. Generate a cryptographically random per-attempt state, store it in the session/pipeline, and validate and consume it on callback.

issues.descricao: The new OAuth step's token exchange and user lookup are not wrapped in error handling, so GitHub/network failures surface as 500s instead of the installation-failed page.

comentarios.texto: The token request is executed outside the try block. If GitHub's token endpoint is unavailable or the request fails with a connection/timeout error, safe_urlopen raises before the guarded response parsing is reached, and this new installation step returns an unhandled server error instead of the installation-failed response. Include the request itself in the error handling and handle the relevant transport exceptions.

WHAT: safe_urlopen token exchange and get_user_info() (which calls resp.raise_for_status()) are called with no exception handling. WHY: Any network error, timeout, or non-2xx from GitHub bubbles up as an unhandled exception and 500s the install instead of rendering the invalid-request page. HOW: Wrap the exchange plus get_user_info in try/except and return error() on failure.

safe_urlopen() and get_user_info() are called outside any try/except, so network errors, non-2xx responses, or API failures raise unhandled exceptions instead of returning error(). Wrap the token exchange + user-info fetch in try/except and return error() on failure, matching the handled missing-access_token path.

issues.descricao: When no Integration exists yet for the installation_id the pipeline advances without comparing the OAuth user to the installer, bypassing the new ownership check.

comentarios.texto: The missing Integration branch advances the pipeline without verifying that github_authenticated_user installed the supplied installation_id. When the installation webhook has not created a record, or the local record was deleted, finish_pipeline calls build_integration using app credentials and attaches the installation without checking the OAuth user's access, allowing a user with another account's installation ID to bypass the new ownership check. Fail closed until trusted installer information is available and apply the ownership check before every successful next_step.

The record-absent path advances the pipeline before checking whether the authenticated GitHub user installed this app. Installation IDs arrive from the request, and a missing Integration record (for example before the installation webhook is processed) does not establish ownership. As a result, this path can attach an installation belonging to a different GitHub user despite the new authenticity check. Verify the authenticated user's authorization for the installation before advancing in this branch too, rather than relying on the webhook-created record existing.

When no Integration row exists for the installation_id, the code calls next_step() without comparing the OAuth-authenticated GitHub user to the installer. An attacker can supply an installation_id they do not own before the installation webhook has created the row, and bypass the new verification. Do not skip the check in this branch. Either fail closed, or verify ownership another way, for example by confirming the user can access the installation through the GitHub API.

issues.descricao: The installer check indexes integration.metadata['sender']['login'] without checking that sender exists, raising KeyError for integrations created without sender metadata.
issues.textoGolden: The code attempts to access integration.metadata[sender][login] without checking for the existence of the sender key. This causes a KeyError for integrations where the sender metadata was not set during creation

comentarios.texto: integration.metadata["sender"]["login"] is indexed without checking that "sender" exists, so an ACTIVE integration whose metadata has no sender raises KeyError (500) here. metadata["sender"] is only populated when state.get("sender") is set (integration.py:376-377), and the only writer of that state is the installation webhook (webhook.py:202-208); integrations created through the pipeline itself carry no sender (confirmed by installation.py:44 which explicitly guards `if "sender" not in integration.metadata`, and by the pipeline-created integration in test_integration.py:730-743). Previously this branch only bound state and called pipeline.next_step(), so this crash is newly introduced. Fix: guard the lookup, e.g. `if pipeline.fetch_state("github_authenticated_user") != (integration.metadata.get("sender") or {}).get("login"):` and decide the desired fallback when sender is absent.

`integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` can raise KeyError. build_integration (line 376-377) only sets metadata["sender"] when state.get("sender") is truthy, so an existing Integration without a sender entry makes this subscripting throw an unhandled KeyError (500) instead of routing to the intended error page. Use `integration.metadata.get("sender", {}).get("login")` (and treat a missing sender as a failed verification) so the mismatch/absence case returns error() rather than crashing.

The new ownership check indexes integration.metadata['sender']['login'] even though GitHubIntegrationProvider.build_integration omits sender for normal pipeline-created integrations. Reconnecting an existing active integration without an OrganizationIntegration and without webhook-populated sender now raises KeyError and returns a server error rather than an installation failure. Handle missing sender explicitly and return the invalid-installation response when trusted installer metadata is unavailable.

issues.descricao: test_installation_not_found uses a wrong OAuth state, so it fails at the state check and never reaches the installation-not-found path it is meant to test.

comentarios.texto: First response (installation_id) is overwritten by second response (bad state) with no assertion, so the Integration.DoesNotExist / not-ACTIVE branch in GitHubInstallation is never verified. Keep/assert the first flow through a valid OAuth step to reach the installation check instead of only asserting the OAuth state-mismatch error.

This test no longer verifies the "installation not found" path it exists for. The second GET supplies state=ddd023d87a913d5226e2a882c4c4cc05, which is not the github pipeline signature (that is the 9cae5e88803f35ed7970fc131e6e65d3 asserted in test_github_setup and reused elsewhere). OAuthLoginView.dispatch (integration.py:412-413) therefore returns error() before GitHubInstallation runs, producing the same generic "Invalid installation request." message and the same failed template via the state-mismatch branch. The Integration.DoesNotExist handling at integration.py:493-498 is never reached, so the test would still pass if that handling were removed or broken. Use the real pipeline state so the request advances into GitHubInstallation, or assert on something that distinguishes the state-mismatch branch from the missing-installation branch.

The replacement assertion no longer verifies that a nonexistent installation is rejected: 'Invalid installation request.' is also returned for a state mismatch, missing access token, or missing authenticated login before GitHubInstallation is reached. This test can therefore pass with installation-not-found handling broken if the callback fails OAuth validation instead. Establish a successful OAuth exchange with the actual pipeline state and verify that the nonexistent installation lookup is reached and rejected, rather than accepting this shared authentication-error message alone.

sugestoes.texto: Pagination is off-by-one when user_count is an exact multiple of limit: totalPages uses Math.floor(user_count / limit) + 1 and next clamps offset to user_count, so a group of 50 members with limit 50 shows page 2/2 and an empty final page. Use Math.ceil(user_count / limit) for totalPages and clamp next to (totalPages - 1) * limit.

members accepts a client-controlled limit with no maximum, so a request such as limit=99999999 can force the server to serialize and return an arbitrarily large member list, causing memory/CPU exhaustion and slow responses on any visible group. Cap limit at a reasonable maximum (e.g., 100).

remove_member deletes the group_users join record immediately with group.users.delete(user_id), then calls group.save. If group.save fails for an unrelated validation reason, the member has already been removed but the server returns a 422, misleading the client. Remove the unnecessary group.save and render success after the delete.

The remove_member automatic-group test sends xhr :put, but config/routes.rb maps remove_member to a DELETE route, so the test does not exercise the endpoint and will fail with a routing error. Change xhr :put to xhr :delete.

removeMember returns bootbox.confirm synchronously, and its callback calls model.removeMember(member) without returning the promise, so async errors are silently ignored and Ember cannot observe the pending operation. Return the removeMember promise from the callback and add an error handler, as the destroy action does.

addMembers does not clear this.usernames after successfully adding members, so clicking Add again re-submits the same users and can hit the unique group_users index. Clear this.set('usernames', null) in the addMembers promise success handler.

findMembers returns undefined when the group name is empty, breaking the old promise contract (previously Ember.RSVP.resolve([])). Any caller or test that chains .then() on the result will throw. Return Ember.RSVP.resolve([]) or Ember.RSVP.resolve() instead.

WHAT: add_members adds every supplied username without checking whether the user is already a group member or whether the same username appears twice. WHY: Group#add pushes onto the has_many :through association, creating a GroupUser join record; the unique DB index on (group_id, user_id) then raises ActiveRecord::RecordNotUnique on duplicates instead of succeeding idempotently, and the per-username loop lacks a transaction so a mid-loop failure can leave partial membership state. HOW: Skip users already in group.user_ids and wrap the additions in a transaction.

WHAT: remove_member deletes the join record with group.users.delete(user_id). WHY: delete on a has_many :through association bypasses GroupUser callbacks, so the user_count counter cache declared on GroupUser is not decremented and the cached member count becomes stale. HOW: Destroy the join record via group.group_users.where(user_id: user_id).destroy_all or group.remove(User.find(user_id)) so the counter-cache callbacks fire.

WHAT: add_members resolves each username with a separate User.find_by_username call inside a loop. WHY: Adding N members performs N user lookups plus N join inserts; the previous usernames= implementation loaded all relevant users in a single User.where(username: ...) query before persisting changes. HOW: Load matching users in one query (User.where(username: usernames.split(','))) and iterate over that result set.

issues.descricao: The admin group pager computes total pages as floor(user_count / limit) + 1, so when the member count is an exact multiple of the limit it shows an extra page and Next navigates to an empty member list.
issues.textoGolden: The `totalPages` calculation using `Math.floor(user_count / limit) + 1` produces an extra page when `user_count` is an exact multiple of `limit`, leading to incorrect pagination. For example, with 100 users and a limit of 50, it reports 3 pages instead of 2, allowing navigation to an empty page.

comentarios.texto: totalPages (and currentPage) use `Math.floor(user_count / limit) + 1`, which is an off-by-one when user_count is an exact multiple of limit (e.g. 50 members, limit 50 → reports 2 pages although only 1 exists). This leaves `showingLast` false on the real last page, so 'next' navigates to an empty page at offset=user_count. Use `Math.ceil(user_count / limit)` (and compute currentPage consistently) to get the correct page count.

totalPages is off by one when user_count is an exact multiple of limit: `Math.floor(user_count / limit) + 1` gives 2 for user_count=50, limit=50, although 50 members occupy exactly one page. Correct it to `Math.ceil(this.get('user_count') / this.get('limit'))`. Effect: for a group whose member count is a multiple of the page size, totalPages is one too high, showingLast remains false so the 'next' link stays enabled, and clicking it navigates to a phantom empty page.

`totalPages` uses `Math.floor(user_count / limit) + 1`, which over-counts by one whenever `user_count` is an exact multiple of `limit` (e.g. 50 members with limit 50 yields 2 pages instead of 1). Since `showingLast` is `propertyEqual("currentPage", "totalPages")`, on a full last page `showingLast` is false, so the `next` action stays enabled and advances `offset` to `user_count`, rendering an empty page labeled as the last page. Use `Math.ceil(user_count / limit)` (with the zero-member guard) so the count matches the real number of pages.

issues.descricao: Several Group model functions (findMembers, destroy, userCountDisplay) return a value on some paths and undefined on others, triggering consistent-return lint warnings.
issues.textoGolden: Expected to return a value at the end of function - code paths without explicit returns will return undefined

issues.descricao: Paging actions fire overlapping member requests and each response unconditionally overwrites offset and members, so a stale response arriving last can revert the list to an earlier page.

comentarios.texto: Guard against stale member-fetch responses before updating the model. `next` updates offset immediately and leaves navigation enabled, so with at least three pages two rapid clicks issue requests for offsets 50 and 100. If the offset-100 response arrives first and the offset-50 response arrives last, this unconditional `setProperties` resets both offset and members to the older page, undoing the latest navigation. Refreshes after membership changes can similarly be overwritten by an earlier fetch. Track a per-model request generation and apply only the latest response, or serialize navigation and refresh requests.

issues.descricao: The public members endpoint now always caps results at 50 per page, but the public group members page has no pagination, so groups with more than 50 members are silently truncated for users.

comentarios.texto: The public members route now loads only the model's default 50-member page without providing any way to request subsequent pages. The public group/members.hbs template only renders members and has no Next/Previous controls, so members after the first 50 become inaccessible (manual groups previously returned all members). Add public pagination controls and actions that update offset and reload members.

The new default limit applies to nonautomatic groups as well, but the public group-members route still calls findMembers() only once and its template simply iterates members without pagination. Previously this endpoint returned every member of a nonautomatic group; now a group with more than 50 members exposes only the first 50 on its public members page, with no way to reach the rest. Update that consumer to fetch subsequent pages or provide pagination when introducing this endpoint contract.

Provide pagination or load subsequent pages for the public group-members view. findMembers now requests only 50 members, and this route calls it only once while its template simply iterates members without navigation. Custom groups previously returned all members, so groups larger than 50 now have members that cannot be viewed on this page.

issues.descricao: Creating a group ignores the alias_level the admin selected, saving only name and visibility, so new groups keep the default alias level.

comentarios.texto: Persist params[:alias_level] when creating a group, just as update does. The creation form exposes aliasLevelOptions and group.asJSON sends the selected alias_level, but create saves only name and visible. A newly created group therefore retains the default alias level instead of the administrator's selection.

issues.descricao: Removing a member deletes the membership row directly and skips clearing the user's primary_group_id, so a removed user can keep this group as their primary group.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: remove_member uses group.users.delete(user_id) instead of the Group#remove destroy path. WHY: bypasses GroupUser destroy callbacks and primary_group_id cleanup done in destroy_deletions, leaving stale membership side-effects (e.g. dangling primary_group_id). HOW: load the User and call group.remove(user).

Removing a member with group.users.delete bypasses the primary_group_id cleanup previously performed by Group#destroy_deletions during usernames updates. A user whose primary group is this group remains associated with it as their primary group after membership removal, leaving stale primary-group state used by user administration and post serialization. Clear primary_group_id for the removed user when it equals this group's id as part of the removal operation.

issues.descricao: The remove_member spec issues a PUT request although the route only maps DELETE to remove_member, so the test uses a verb never routed in production.
issues.textoGolden: The remove_member test uses xhr :put to call the remove_member action, but the route defines delete 'members' => 'groups#remove_member' requiring DELETE method.

comentarios.texto: This example sends `xhr :put, :remove_member`, but the PR maps `remove_member` only to DELETE (`delete "members" => "groups#remove_member"`); PUT on that path routes to `groups#add_members`. Controller specs bypass the router, so the example still lands on `remove_member` and passes regardless — it would still pass if the DELETE route were missing or wired to the wrong action, leaving the newly introduced verb/action pairing untested. Use `xhr :delete, :remove_member`, as the sibling example at line 125 already does.

The test 'cannot remove members from automatic groups' sends `xhr :put, :remove_member`, but the route is `delete "members" => "groups#remove_member"`. It exercises the action with a verb that is never routed in production. Use `xhr :delete, :remove_member, group_id: 1, user_id: 42` so the test matches the real request.

issues.descricao: Admin add_members pushes every username into group.users without skipping existing members, so adding someone already in the group hits the unique group_users index, returns a 500 and leaves earlier users partially added.
The public group members endpoint takes `limit` from params with no upper bound or positivity check, letting a visitor request huge pages or trigger a 500 with a negative limit.
Admin remove_member calls group.users.delete with a raw integer id, which raises RecordNotFound (404/500) when the user is not or no longer a member, e.g. on concurrent removal.
Admin remove_member deletes memberships with group.users.delete, which skips GroupUser callbacks, so the cached groups.user_count is never decremented and stays inflated.
Group member pagination is off by one when user_count is a multiple of limit: Next moves to offset == user_count and shows an empty page.
`add_members` runs one User query per username; load all users with a single `User.where(username: ...)` query.

sugestoes.texto: The retryCount branch of the deleteMany OR is not scoped to WorkflowMethods.SMS, so it deletes WorkflowReminder rows of any method (EMAIL, WHATSAPP) whose retryCount is greater than 1. Add `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS` to that branch to preserve the original SMS-only cleanup semantics.

The catch block increments retryCount even when the error came from the prisma.workflowReminder.update calls inside the if/else branches. This causes a double increment when the retryCount update fails (0 → 2 in one pass) and incorrectly marks a successfully-scheduled SMS as failed when the success update fails. Move the retryCount update outside the catch or guard it so it only runs for scheduling failures, not for DB-update failures.

twilio.scheduleSMS returns undefined when SMS sending is locked, and the new else branch treats that as a scheduling failure and increments retryCount. Because locks are typically temporary/administrative states, legitimate reminders get deleted after two cron runs. Distinguish a lock return from a real scheduling failure and do not count locks toward the retry limit.

The new deleteMany query uses `retryCount: { gt: 1 }` in an OR clause, but WorkflowReminder has no index on retryCount. On a large table the unindexed disjunct can force a sequential scan. Add an index on retryCount (e.g., `@@index([retryCount])`) so the cleanup query stays efficient.

WHAT: The cleanup deleteMany deletes any WorkflowReminder with retryCount > 1, regardless of method. WHY: This cron job is scoped to SMS, but the unscoped OR branch will also delete email or WhatsApp reminders if they ever use retryCount. HOW: Add method: WorkflowMethods.SMS to the retryCount branch of the OR clause.

WHAT: twilio.scheduleSMS returns undefined when the user/team is locked for SMS sending, and the new else branch increments retryCount as if scheduling failed. WHY: Lock state is a business/permission condition, not a transient failure; after two cron runs the valid reminder is permanently deleted even though the account may later be unlocked. HOW: Do not increment retryCount when the undefined return comes from the SMS lock path, e.g., distinguish lock from an actual provider error.

WHAT: The catch block increments retryCount for any error thrown in the try block, including failures of prisma.workflowReminder.update after Twilio already returned a successful scheduledSMS. WHY: A successfully-sent SMS whose state update fails is treated as a scheduling failure, causing a duplicate send on retry and eventual deletion of a valid reminder. HOW: Move the success-state update into its own error-handling path so a post-send DB write failure does not increment retryCount.

WHAT: The new deleteMany filter retryCount: { gt: 1 } has no supporting database index. WHY: On a large WorkflowReminder table the cron cleanup will perform a sequential scan every run, causing a material slowdown and holding locks during deletion. HOW: Add an index on retryCount to WorkflowReminder, such as @@index([retryCount]) or @@index([method, retryCount]).

issues.descricao: retryCount is set to reminder.retryCount + 1 from a value read at the start of the run instead of an atomic increment, so overlapping runs can lose increments.
issues.textoGolden: Using retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1 reads a possibly stale value and can lose increments under concurrency; consider an atomic increment via Prisma (increment: 1) to avoid race conditions (also applies to the similar update in the catch block).

comentarios.texto: WHAT: retryCount is incremented with a read-value computed at the start of the run (`retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1`) instead of an atomic increment. WHY: if two cron invocations overlap (or the same reminder is processed twice before the write commits), both read the same retryCount and both write N+1, so failures are undercounted and the reminder can loop forever without ever reaching the `retryCount > 1` deletion threshold. HOW: use `data: { retryCount: { increment: 1 } }` so the increment is atomic (the initial read value is then irrelevant).

`retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1` is a read-modify-write of the value fetched at the top of the handler, not an atomic increment. Two overlapping cron runs both read the same retryCount and both write the same +1, losing an update, so failed reminders can be retried indefinitely and never reach the `gt: 1` deletion threshold. Use Prisma's atomic `retryCount: { increment: 1 }` instead of computing from the stale in-memory value (same issue in the else branch at lines 179-186).

Retry counts are assigned from the stale findMany snapshot instead of incremented atomically, both here and in the catch branch. Two overlapping cron requests can each fail scheduling the same reminder with retryCount zero and both write one, so two failed attempts do not reach the deletion threshold and additional attempts are scheduled. Use Prisma's atomic retryCount increment operation in both failure branches.

issues.descricao: The deleteMany OR clause applies retryCount > 1 without the SMS method filter, so the SMS cron deletes any workflow reminder (email, WhatsApp) with retryCount above 1.
issues.textoGolden: The deletion logic in scheduleSMSReminders.ts incorrectly deletes non-SMS workflow reminders (e.g., Email, WhatsApp) that have retryCount > 1. This occurs because the retryCount condition within the OR clause for deletion lacks a method: WorkflowMethods.SMS filter, causing it to apply to all reminder types instead of only SMS reminders, which is the intended scope of this function.

comentarios.texto: The comment "//delete all scheduled sms reminders where scheduled date is past current date" no longer describes the deleteMany below it. After this change the query also deletes reminders with retryCount > 1, and that OR branch has no `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS` filter, so non-SMS (email) reminders with retryCount > 1 are now deleted too. Update the comment (or add the missing SMS filter to the retryCount branch) so the prose matches what the code actually deletes.
The deleteMany OR clause deletes any reminder with retryCount > 1 regardless of method.

The second OR branch `{ retryCount: { gt: 1 } }` has no `method` filter, unlike the first branch (`method: WorkflowMethods.SMS`). Because `retryCount` is a generic column on WorkflowReminder used by all reminder methods, this deleteMany now permanently deletes every reminder of ANY method (including EMAIL) whose retryCount exceeds 1, even though this cron is only supposed to clean up SMS reminders. Add `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS` to this branch (or scope the whole where to SMS) so non-SMS reminders are never destroyed.

issues.descricao: The cleanup comment describes only past-date SMS deletion and omits the new retryCount > 1 deletion branch.

comentarios.texto: Update the cleanup comment to describe the new retry-exhaustion deletion branch. It currently says this deletes scheduled SMS reminders whose date has passed, but this OR branch also deletes any reminder with retryCount > 1, including future-dated reminders and without an SMS restriction. The comment now misrepresents the scope of this destructive operation.

Stale comment: line 28 says 'delete all scheduled sms reminders where scheduled date is past current date' but the new OR clause also deletes any reminder with retryCount > 1 regardless of method or date. Update the comment to describe both branches.

issues.descricao: The retry-count update inside the catch block is not guarded, so if it throws (for example the reminder was deleted concurrently) the error escapes the loop and the cron run fails, skipping the remaining reminders.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: the catch block performs an unguarded `prisma.workflowReminder.update` while handling the scheduling error. WHY: if this write itself rejects (e.g. the row was concurrently removed, or a transient DB error), the rejection is not caught and escapes the for-loop, aborting the whole cron run so all remaining reminders go unprocessed. HOW: wrap the retryCount update in its own try/catch (log and continue) so a failure to record the retry does not abort processing of the remaining reminders.

This new `prisma.workflowReminder.update` sits inside the catch block, which is NOT protected by any try/catch. If this update throws (e.g. the reminder was already removed by the `deleteMany` at the top of the file during a concurrent run -> Prisma P2025, or a transient DB error), the exception escapes the `for` loop and rejects the handler, so all remaining unscheduled reminders are skipped and the cron request fails. Previously the catch only did `console.log`, so a single bad reminder never aborted the batch and the endpoint always returned 200. Wrap this update in its own try/catch (or `updateMany`/catch-and-log) so a failed retry-count write cannot take down the whole scheduling run.

The new database update inside catch can itself throw when a reminder has been deleted during scheduling. Booking cancellation deletes reminders through handleCancelBooking and deleteScheduledSMSReminder, so a concurrent cancellation followed by a scheduling error now rejects the entire cron handler and prevents the remaining reminders from being processed. Use an updateMany filtered by the reminder ID to tolerate an already-deleted row, and guard errors from retry bookkeeping so they do not escape the per-reminder error handler.

issues.descricao: Claims transient errors increment retryCount, so two runs during an outage delete the whole pending SMS reminder queue.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: The catch block unconditionally increments retryCount for any exception (profile/bookerUrl/templating/rate-limit/Twilio outage). WHY: Two consecutive cron runs with a transient global failure increment every pending SMS reminder to 2 and the startup deleteMany then wipes the entire future SMS queue, not just permanently-invalid numbers. HOW: Only increment on permanent scheduleSMS failure, or distinguish transient errors from terminal ones before counting toward deletion.

issues.descricao: The new OR arm on retryCount has no supporting index, so the cleanup delete can no longer be fully served by the existing index and may scan the table.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: the deleteMany WHERE now uses `OR` between `(method = SMS AND scheduledDate <= now)` and `retryCount > 1`, but WorkflowReminder has no index on the newly added retryCount column. WHY: Postgres cannot satisfy a two-way OR using the existing (method, scheduled, scheduledDate) index and will fall back to a sequential scan of the entire WorkflowReminder table on every cron invocation, turning a previously indexed delete into a full table scan as the table grows. HOW: add an index on retryCount (or restructure so each branch is index-usable), then re-check the query plan.

issues.descricao: The retryCount increment update is duplicated in the else branch and the catch block.

comentarios.texto: The retryCount increment is duplicated in the else-branch and catch.

issues.descricao: SMS-sending locks are counted as failed scheduling attempts: scheduleSMS returns undefined for locked users/teams, retryCount is incremented, and after two cron runs the retryCount > 1 cleanup deletes future reminders even if sending is later unlocked.
retryCount is not incremented when a reminder has no message or no sendTo number, so such reminders are reprocessed on every cron run until their scheduled date.

sugestoes.texto: readLength() validates `length >= limit` where `limit` is the total input array size, not the remaining bytes. This lets malformed lengths that are larger than the remaining stream but smaller than the total array pass validation, so parsing fails only later with EOF instead of being rejected early. Compare against the actual remaining bytes (e.g., `is.available()`) or track remaining bytes explicitly.

readLength() returns `-1` for indefinite-length encoding, but readSequence() interprets `-1` as zero content and returns an empty list, while readInteger() would call `read(-1)` and throw NegativeArraySizeException. Reject indefinite-length encoding with an IOException in readLength(), or handle the sentinel explicitly in both callers.

readLength validates length against the total array size (`limit`) instead of the bytes remaining in the stream. A malformed length that exceeds the remaining bytes but is smaller than the total input passes the check, so readSequence can over-consume trailing bytes and the caller gets a generic EOF/IO error instead of an early out-of-bounds rejection. Track remaining bytes (`limit - count`) and reject `length > remaining`.

readLength returns -1 for indefinite-length encoding, and readSequence treats -1 as zero content and returns an empty list. Since this decoder is intended for DER (definite-length) ECDSA signatures, indefinite-length input should be rejected explicitly; otherwise a malformed/BER sequence is silently parsed as empty before the caller's size check fires.

issues.descricao: concatenatedRSToASN1DER encodes r and s into two throwaway ASN1Encoder instances before re-encoding them in the return statement.
issues.textoGolden: Dead code exists where ASN1Encoder instances are created and written to, but their results are immediately discarded. The actual encoding is performed by new ASN1Encoder instances created in the subsequent return statement, rendering the earlier operations useless.

comentarios.texto: Dead computation: the two ASN1Encoder.create().write(...) calls allocate encoders and encode rBigInteger/sBigInteger, but their results are discarded — the returned DER comes entirely from the expression at lines 117-121, which re-encodes the same BigIntegers. These two statements have no effect and should be removed (they are a leftover from an earlier formulation).

Remove these two discarded encoder writes. Each allocates an encoder and encodes a BigInteger, but neither result participates in the returned signature; lines 119–120 repeat both writes on fresh encoders. This performs redundant encoding and allocations on every concatenated-signature conversion.

The two statements `ASN1Encoder.create().write(rBigInteger);` and `ASN1Encoder.create().write(sBigInteger);` encode values and discard the results. The return expression re-encodes the same values, so these lines are dead computation left over from a copy-paste or refactor. Remove them.

issues.descricao: order() is added to CryptoProvider as an abstract method, breaking source and binary compatibility for existing third-party CryptoProvider implementations.
issues.textoGolden: Abstract order() method on CryptoProvider may break backward compatibility with existing implementations

comentarios.texto: order() was added as an abstract method to the public CryptoProvider interface. CryptoIntegration.detectProvider now invokes order() on every ServiceLoader-discovered CryptoProvider via Comparator.comparingInt(CryptoProvider::order). Any CryptoProvider implementation compiled against the previous interface (an external or separately built provider jar on the classpath) will throw AbstractMethodError at detection time, i.e. during AuthzClient.create()/server bootstrap, before any provider is usable. Giving order() a default implementation (e.g. default int order() { return 0; }) avoids the binary-incompatibility.

issues.descricao: detectProvider no longer fails when several crypto providers are present; with Default, FIPS and Elytron all at order 200, ties are resolved by classpath order and a FIPS deployment can silently run with the non-FIPS provider.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: detectProvider sorts by order() reversed and silently picks index 0, removing the previous multiple-providers error. WHY: Default/FIPS/Elytron all return order 200, so ambiguous classpath (e.g. default+FIPS) now nondeterministically picks one by ServiceLoader order instead of failing fast, risking wrong FIPS vs non-FIPS crypto. HOW: only auto-ignore lower-order providers; throw when the top two have equal order().

Reject ambiguous highest-priority providers rather than silently taking the first. Both DefaultCryptoProvider and FIPS1402Provider return order 200 in this PR, so when both are present the stable sort leaves the decision to ServiceLoader discovery order. A deployment expecting FIPS can therefore initialize the ordinary Bouncy Castle provider without an error; previously this mixed classpath failed closed. Preserve the error for tied highest-priority providers (or require an explicit security-mode/provider choice), while still allowing the lower-priority authz-client fallback.

detectProvider() no longer fails fast when multiple CryptoProviders are present and instead silently picks the first after sorting by order() descending. All Keycloak providers return the same order (DefaultCryptoProvider, FIPS1402Provider, WildFlyElytronProvider all return 200), so a tie between two providers is broken by the non-deterministic ServiceLoader iteration order rather than the intended priority. The previous code threw an IllegalStateException forcing the classpath to be corrected; now a deployment with two provider jars (exactly the 'multiple providers on classpath' scenario this PR enables) can silently select the unintended provider — e.g. a non-FIPS/strict provider when FIPS is required — with no error. Use a stable tie-breaker (delegate to the provider name/type) or reject equal top orders instead of relying on ServiceLoader order.

issues.descricao: Claims a wrong-length JOSE signature causes an unchecked exception in concatenatedRSToASN1DER; verifiers catch it and report verification failure, as with the existing providers.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: concatenatedRSToASN1DER splits signature without validating signature.length==signLength. WHY: short JOSE input throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException and long input is silently truncated to signLength, breaking the ECDSACryptoProvider contract (IOException on malformed) used by verifier contexts. HOW: check length upfront and throw IOException.

concatenatedRSToASN1DER never validates signature.length == signLength before System.arraycopy(signature,0,r,1,len) / (signature,len,s,1,len). A short JWS signature throws unchecked ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException instead of the declared IOException, breaking verification on attacker-controlled input. Validate length and throw IOException.

issues.descricao: The ES384 and ES512 tests sign with the same default P-256 key, so the converter is never tested with real P-384 or P-521 signatures.

comentarios.texto: Single default EC keypair reused for ES256/ES384/ES512: testES384/testES512 names claim larger curves but body signs with the same P-256 key and only pads to larger signLength, so full-width 384/521-bit handling is never exercised. Generate a per-algorithm keypair with the correct curve (e.g. secp256r1/secp384r1/secp521r1) before signing.

Every case generates a default EC key rather than a key on the curve associated with the named algorithm. On the standard JDK this is P-256, so testES384 and testES512 just pad P-256 signature components to larger lengths. A converter that discards nonzero high bytes beyond 32 bytes would still pass all three cases. Initialize the key generator with the appropriate curve per case (P-256, P-384, and P-521) so the larger-component conversions are actually tested.

Generate a key on the curve corresponding to each tested algorithm rather than using the provider's default EC curve for all three tests. On the standard JDK this generates a P-256 key even for testES384 and testES512, so those tests merely pad P-256 integers to larger output lengths and never exercise actual P-384/P-521 signature encoding (including P-521's long-form sequence length).

issues.descricao: The test only checks a round trip between the two new converters and never verifies the re-encoded DER against the original signature or with Signature.verify, so mutually consistent bugs go undetected.

comentarios.texto: Tautological round-trip assertion: rsConcat2 is derived from rsConcat via encode+decode that are inverses if self-consistent, so assertArrayEquals(rsConcat,rsConcat2) passes even if both directions are wrong. Verify against external oracle: Signature.initVerify + verify(asn1Des) and/or compare rsConcat to expected split, not just to itself.

The test only checks self-consistency: it asserts asn1derToConcatenatedRS(g(asn1derToConcatenatedRS(sign))) == asn1derToConcatenatedRS(sign), i.e. that concatenatedRSToASN1DER is a right inverse of asn1derToConcatenatedRS. It never compares against the original DER `sign`, never verifies the ECDSA signature, and never asserts the emvider output is canonical DER. Because the decoder it reads back with (ASN1Decoder.readLength) accepts non-canonical long-form lengths (e.g. 0x81) and validates only tag numbers, a regression in ASN1Encoder.writeLength that always emitted long form would still round-trip and the test would still pass, even though the produced signature would no longer be valid DER and would be rejected by the Keycloak server / a JDK Signature.verify. Assert the encoded signature is valid DER (e.g. verify it with a JDK Signature, or compare asn1derToConcatenatedRS(sign) against a known-good width-padded r||s and assert its length equals algorithm.getSignatureLength()).

The assertion only establishes agreement between the two new conversion routines, not correctness of the converted signature. For example, swapping r and s in both routines makes this entire round trip pass, although the DER result no longer verifies the signed data. Verify `asn1Des` with the public key and original data (or compare against an independently specified encoding) so mutually compensating conversion defects fail the test.

issues.descricao: getBouncyCastleProvider in AuthzClientCryptoProvider returns the JDK default KeyStore provider instead of BouncyCastle, contrary to the CryptoProvider contract.
ASN1Decoder.readInteger accepts constructed INTEGER tags because it only masks the low tag bits, so malformed DER is parsed as valid.

sugestoes.texto: OptimizedCursorPaginator is hard-coded for integer keys but is used with a DateTimeField. get_item_key calls math.floor/ceil on the raw datetime value, which raises TypeError, and value_from_cursor returns the numeric cursor value instead of a datetime so build_queryset compares the datetime column to the wrong type. Use datetime-aware key conversion (like DateTimePaginator) when ordering by datetime, or use DateTimePaginator as the base for this endpoint.

The negative-offset branch passes a negative start index to queryset slicing (e.g., queryset[cursor.offset:...]). Django QuerySet slicing does not support negative start indices and raises an exception, so a caller-supplied cursor with a negative offset will 500 instead of enabling efficient reverse pagination. Either reject/ignore negative offsets or implement reverse pagination by flipping the ordering and cursor value, not by negative slicing.

OptimizedCursorPaginator assumes numeric order_by keys but OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint uses it with order_by='-datetime'. get_item_key calls math.floor/ceil on a datetime, which raises TypeError when build_cursor generates next/prev cursors; value_from_cursor returns a raw numeric cursor value that is then compared against a datetime column in build_queryset. Either make this paginator datetime-aware (like DateTimePaginator) or do not use it for datetime-ordered audit logs.

The 'advanced' negative-offset branch passes a negative start index to Django QuerySet slicing (queryset[cursor.offset:...]), which raises AssertionError because Django does not support negative indexing on QuerySets. Remove or replace this branch with a valid bounded implementation; the current code will crash for any admin/superuser who supplies a negative cursor offset.

organization_context.member.has_global_access is dereferenced without a None check, but RpcUserOrganizationContext.member is documented as nullable when the user has no membership in the organization. For non-superusers where member is None this raises AttributeError. Guard the access with getattr(organization_context.member, 'has_global_access', False) or a None check.

issues.descricao: OptimizedCursorPaginator passes negative cursor offsets straight into Django queryset slicing, which Django does not support, so requests with a negative offset raise an error instead of returning a page.
issues.textoGolden: The OptimizedCursorPaginator in organization_auditlogs.py attempts to use negative slice offsets on Django querysets, but Django querysets do not support negative slicing and will raise an AssertionError.

comentarios.texto: The advanced negative-offset branch passes a negative slice start directly to a Django QuerySet, which does not support negative indexing. A cursor such as 0:-1:0 is accepted by Cursor.from_string but crashes the optimized audit-log request instead of providing reverse pagination. Reject negative offsets with BadPaginationError or implement reverse traversal using nonnegative slices and reversed ordering.

The comment claiming that Django ORM 'properly handles negative slicing automatically' is false: Django QuerySet slicing rejects negative indices. This branch passes cursor.offset straight into queryset[start_offset:stop], so it raises rather than supplying the documented negative-offset pagination. Correct the negative-offset support claims here, in the class docstring, and in the new BasePaginator boundary-handling comment (or implement actual supported boundary handling) so callers are not promised a pagination mode that the underlying queryset cannot provide.

Django QuerySets do not support negative slice bounds. Passing a negative cursor offset directly into `queryset[start_offset:stop]` raises an exception instead of enabling advanced pagination. Validate or normalize negative offsets before slicing, or implement reverse traversal through ordering/filtering rather than negative slices.

issues.descricao: The comment added to BasePaginator claims negative offsets are allowed and safely handled by the queryset, but the code clamps non-prev offsets to zero and leaves prev offsets as before, so the comment misdescribes the behaviour.

comentarios.texto: The added comment says this change will "allow negative offsets to enable efficient bidirectional pagination ... safe because the underlying queryset will handle boundary conditions", but the statement it annotates, line 182, is `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` — it clamps negative offsets to 0, i.e. it does the opposite of what the comment claims and leaves the 'negative offset' (offset < 0) paging behaviour exactly as before. The comment is now untrue for the code it sits on; either drop the 'allow negative offsets' wording or make the code actually permit them.

The comment declares this change `allow[s] negative offsets to enable efficient bidirectional pagination`, but the actual computation is `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset`, which clamps non-prev offsets at 0 — i.e. it never permits a negative offset. The declared optimization is a no-op relative to the original `queryset[offset:stop]`; the comment describes behavior the code does not have.

BasePaginator now passes the raw `offset` to the slice whenever `cursor.is_prev` is true (`max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset`). A negative offset from a user-supplied prev cursor therefore reaches `queryset[negative:stop]`, which Django rejects. This crashes every endpoint that uses BasePaginator. Fix: always use `max(0, offset)`, or validate the offset when the cursor is parsed.

issues.descricao: The OptimizedCursorPaginator docstring claims streamlined boundary handling, an optimized query path and backward compatibility that the implementation, a copy of BasePaginator plus a negative-offset branch, does not provide.

comentarios.texto: Docstring lists 'Streamlined boundary condition handling', 'Optimized query path for large datasets', and 'maintaining backward compatibility', but get_result (845-886) is a copy of BasePaginator with only a negative-offset branch added — no streamlined handling or optimized path exists, and negative-offset slicing breaks prior cursor semantics. Doc describes behavior the function does not produce — align doc to code or implement the claimed handling.

issues.descricao: OptimizedCursorPaginator computes cursor keys with math.floor/ceil on the raw attribute, but the audit log endpoint uses it with order_by='-datetime', so building the cursor raises TypeError for any non-empty result.
issues.textoGolden: get_item_key assumes a numeric key, but the paginator is used with order_by=-datetime in the audit logs endpoint; calling math.floor/ceil on a datetime will raise a TypeError.

comentarios.texto: OptimizedCursorPaginator requires numeric integer keys (get_item_key uses math.floor/ceil + int, cursor_value defaults to 0) but is instantiated here with order_by="-datetime". This mismatched producer/consumer contract breaks pagination for datetime-ordered audit logs. Fix: do not use OptimizedCursorPaginator for datetime ordering; keep DateTimePaginator or make OptimizedCursorPaginator datetime-aware.

WHAT: OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key/value_from_cursor mishandles datetime ordering by calling math.floor/ceil directly on a datetime and returning raw int cursor value. WHY: Used with order_by="-datetime" it crashes with TypeError on floor(datetime) when building cursors and filters the datetime column against an int in build_queryset, breaking pagination. HOW: Copy DateTimePaginator logic — timestamp via strftime/multiplier with floor/ceil and convert cursor value back with datetime.fromtimestamp.

The optimized branch selects a numeric-key paginator while ordering by the datetime field. On any nonempty first page, build_cursor invokes OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key, which calls math.ceil on a datetime and raises TypeError; nonzero cursors also lack the datetime conversion provided by DateTimePaginator. Make the optimized paginator inherit DateTimePaginator or preserve its timestamp encoding and decoding.

issues.descricao: The audit log endpoint always dereferences organization_context.member.has_global_access, which crashes with AttributeError for authorized token requests that have no member, even on the default pagination path.
issues.textoGolden: When requests are authenticated with API keys or org auth tokens (which have user_id=None), organization_context.member is None. Line 71 attempts to access organization_context.member.has_global_access without checking if member is None, causing an AttributeError crash when optimized_pagination=true is used, even though the request passed all permission checks with valid org:write scope.

comentarios.texto: The unconditional advanced-access check dereferences organization_context.member although RpcUserOrganizationContext permits member=None. Authorized non-member organization-token requests therefore raise AttributeError even when optimized_pagination is absent, instead of returning audit logs through the existing paginator. Guard the optional member and evaluate eligibility only when optimized pagination is requested.

issues.descricao: The comments and enable_advanced variable describe the optimized_pagination path as a performance optimization for administrators, hiding that it enables negative-offset slicing.

comentarios.texto: The comments describe a 'performance optimization' for 'authorized administrators', and the variable is named enable_advanced. In fact it opts into negative-offset slicing, and the optimized_pagination query parameter gates it. The names and comments hide what the flag actually enables. Rename them to say what is enabled, or remove the path.

issues.descricao: A user-controlled optimized_pagination flag lets any member with global access switch to a paginator that accepts unvalidated negative cursor offsets, widening the attack surface and causing server errors.

comentarios.texto: A user-controlled `optimized_pagination` query flag switches the endpoint to a paginator that accepts attacker-supplied negative cursor offsets. This is available to any user with global access, not only to real admins. It widens the attack surface for unvalidated cursor offsets and causes server errors. The comment 'permissions are checked at the queryset level' is not backed by any check in the paginator. Fix: remove the optimized path, or have the paginator validate and clamp offsets.

issues.descricao: BasePaginator.get_result clamps negative offsets only for next cursors; a prev cursor with a negative offset is passed straight into the queryset slice, which Django rejects with an error (500) on every paginated endpoint.
The new comment in Cursor says negative offsets are allowed to enable efficient reverse pagination, but the constructor only calls int(offset) and provides no such behaviour.
OptimizedCursorPaginator.value_from_cursor returns the raw integer cursor value, which is then compared against the datetime column, so next/prev cursor pagination of audit logs breaks.
Comments in OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result claim Django handles negative slicing and that permissions are checked at the queryset level; both are false.

sugestoes.texto: Rescheduling calls `deleteScheduledEmailReminder(reminder.id, reminder.referenceId, true)`, which cancels the SendGrid send but does not delete the WorkflowReminder row or mark it `cancelled`. The original booking is only updated to CANCELLED, so cascade delete does not remove the row, leaving orphaned email reminder rows (SMS reminders in the same loop are deleted). Delete the row after successful cancellation, or use the non-immediate path so the cron cleans it up.

Async cancellation helpers are invoked inside `Array.forEach` without awaiting. The email helper persists `cancelled: true`, which the cron relies on to cancel the SendGrid send. If the handler returns before the Prisma update completes (e.g., serverless freeze), the cron will not cancel the email and the cancelled booking can still receive the reminder. Replace `forEach` with `Promise.all`/`for...of await` and include the promises in the final `Promise.all`.

Async cancellation helpers are invoked inside `Array.forEach` without awaiting, so the immediate SendGrid cancel request may not complete before the handler returns. The surrounding `try/catch` also cannot catch errors from async `forEach` callbacks. If the cancellation is lost, the previous rescheduled booking still receives its scheduled email. Replace `forEach` with `Promise.all`/`for...of await` and await the cancellations.

WHAT: The async cancellation helpers deleteScheduledEmailReminder and deleteScheduledSMSReminder are called inside Array.forEach without awaiting, and their Promises are not collected into the Promise.all at line 497. WHY: The handler can return before the Prisma update that sets cancelled=true (or the SMS delete) is persisted; in a serverless environment the pending work may never complete, so the cron job does not see the reminders as cancelled and still sends the workflow emails for cancelled bookings. HOW: Collect the returned Promises (e.g. with Promise.all(updatedBookings.flatMap(...))) and await them before the final Promise.all/prisma cleanup.

WHAT: During rescheduling, deleteScheduledEmailReminder(..., true) and deleteScheduledSMSReminder are fired inside Array.forEach without awaiting, and the wrapping try/catch cannot catch errors from those asynchronous calls. WHY: The immediate SendGrid cancel and Twilio cancel may not complete before the API response is sent; if the environment is frozen the old booking’s workflow emails are still sent. The try/catch also fails to log failures because forEach does not return the async errors. HOW: Replace forEach with a loop or Promise.all over the reminders and await the cancellation results inside the existing try/catch.

WHAT: The immediateDelete branch in deleteScheduledEmailReminder posts the SendGrid cancel request and returns without updating or deleting the WorkflowReminder row. WHY: Callers that pass immediateDelete=true (e.g. handleNewBooking rescheduling) leave stale scheduled reminders in the database with scheduled=true and cancelled unset; those rows are never matched by the cron cancellation query and persist until their scheduledDate passes, causing incorrect data and confusing future cancellation attempts. HOW: After a successful SendGrid cancel in the immediateDelete branch, delete the WorkflowReminder row (consistent with deleteScheduledSMSReminder) or set cancelled=true so the cron can clean it up.

issues.descricao: Reminder cancel helpers are called without await inside forEach when bookings are cancelled/rescheduled or workflows edited, so the handler can return before reminders are cancelled or deleted and failures are unobserved.
issues.textoGolden: Asynchronous functions deleteScheduledEmailReminder and deleteScheduledSMSReminder are called without await inside forEach loops. This occurs during booking rescheduling/cancellation, and workflow/workflow step deletion/updates. Consequently, scheduled workflow reminders may not be reliably cancelled, potentially leaving them active.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: async deleteScheduledEmailReminder/deleteScheduledSMSReminder called inside forEach without collecting/awaiting promises. WHY: handler returns before cancels complete and rejections are unobserved, so cancellations are lost and reminder emails/SMS are still sent (same fire-and-forget pattern repeated in handleNewBooking:966, bookings.tsx:488, workflows.tsx:212/376/519/574).

Cancellation now delegates the database update/deletion to asynchronous reminder helpers without awaiting them, while removing reminder deletes from the awaited promise list. The handler can finish before cancelled flags or unscheduled-reminder deletions are persisted, allowing a subsequent scheduler run to schedule a cancelled booking's reminder and leaving cancellation work unfinished when a serverless invocation terminates. Collect and await the helper promises; apply the same correction to the modified rescheduling and workflow-update callers that discard these promises.

Await the reminder cancellation promises before completing the cancellation request. These helpers now own persistence of cancellation: email awaits a workflowReminder update and SMS awaits Twilio before deleting the row. The forEach discards their promises, and removing remindersToDelete from the awaited promise list removes the previous guarantee that reminder state is cleared before the handler returns. In a serverless request the outstanding operations can be interrupted after the response, leaving reminders active for a cancelled booking. Collect these helper promises and include them in the awaited Promise.all.

issues.descricao: The cron cancels SendGrid sends for cancelled reminders in one try around the whole loop, so one failing cancel aborts all remaining cancellations and the row deletions, and the failing row blocks later runs.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: remindersToCancel loop awaits SendGrid cancel per-reminder inside one try and only runs Prisma deletes after the loop, with no method filter. WHY: a single throw (e.g. null SMS referenceId sent as batch_id, or one SendGrid error) aborts the loop and skips Promise.all deletes, leaving all other cancelled emails still scheduled so they are still sent.

Successful cancellation records are only deleted after every SendGrid request in the loop succeeds. If a later request fails, the catch skips all queued Prisma deletions; the next run retries an already-cancelled batch, which SendGrid rejects with 400, and aborts before processing the remaining reminders. Await each reminder's database deletion immediately after its successful cancellation and isolate errors per reminder so one failed batch does not block the others.

Handle cancellation failures per reminder rather than around the entire batch. If one SendGrid request rejects (for example, for an expired or invalid batch ID), the loop exits before cancelling the remaining reminders, and Promise.all is never reached, so even earlier successfully cancelled reminders remain in the database. The failed record stays eligible for the next run and can repeatedly block other cancellations until their emails are sent. Execute each successful deletion and isolate failures so the worker continues processing the remaining reminders.

issues.descricao: Email reminders for cancelled bookings are only flagged cancelled and cancelled in SendGrid by the cron later, so reminders close to their send time can still be delivered.

comentarios.texto: Deferred cancellation includes reminders less than ten minutes from their scheduled send time, when SendGrid no longer permits cancellation. A booking cancelled in that interval is only marked cancelled locally by deleteScheduledEmailReminder, and the cron's POST is rejected, so its email is still delivered. Process cancellation before SendGrid's ten-minute cutoff and explicitly handle cancellations that arrive after that deadline rather than relying on this cron query to stop delivery.

issues.descricao: The cron cancels SendGrid scheduled sends one at a time with sequential awaits, which is slower than batching.

comentarios.texto: The new cancel loop performs a sequentially awaited SendGrid HTTP request (`await client.request(...)`) for each reminder returned by an unbounded `findMany` (no `take`), then deletes them.
